title: When hardware misbehaves
summary: Connect power, memory, and thermal symptoms.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: A computer that shuts down under load may be protecting itself from excessive temperature, but the symptom alone does not identify the faulty part. Record when the shutdown happens and inspect safe, observable evidence such as fan operation, airflow, and reported temperatures. A machine with no power needs a different starting point: verify the outlet, external cable, power switch, and appropriate supply connections before blaming the operating system.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: POST signals can narrow a startup failure, but their meaning depends on the manufacturer and model. Look up the documented code rather than assuming every beep pattern is universal. Intermittent crashes can involve memory, power, heat, drivers, or applications, so change one variable at a time and test the result. If there is smoke or a burning smell, stop testing and follow electrical safety procedures. Never open a power supply to investigate its internals; hazardous stored energy can remain after unplugging it.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
